query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is primarily governed by grain boundary–mediated oxidation that forms a nonuniform, Cr‐enriched protective oxide scale whose stability is critically sensitive to the ambient gas environment. In oxidizing atmospheres the initially protective Cr-rich layer develops internal stresses and spalls over time, while in reducing environments the incomplete or destabilized oxide scale accelerates compositional degradation at the exposed grain boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: As-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous FCC matrix and minimal pre-existing oxide on the surface.
generation.intervention: Expose identical alloy samples to high-temperature (e.g., ~900 °C) aging treatments in controlled oxidizing (e.g., oxygen-rich) and reducing (e.g., hydrogen or inert with reducing potential) gas atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (around 900 °C), defined exposure times (e.g., up to 120 hours), and precisely controlled gas compositions to contrast oxidizing versus reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that serve as fast diffusion paths for oxygen leading to localized formation of a Cr-rich oxide scale, along with minor contributions from Al and Ti forming secondary oxide phases.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, oxygen diffuses preferentially along grain boundaries, oxidizing Cr to form a layered (initially protective) oxide. Under oxidizing conditions, thermal stresses and volume mismatch between the oxide scale and the FCC matrix eventually lead to spallation. In a reducing atmosphere, the subdued oxidation reaction produces an unstable or incomplete oxide scale, permitting continued elemental depletion and microstructural changes that degrade surface integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: In oxidizing conditions, there will be an initial mass gain from oxide formation that later declines as spallation degrades the surface integrity, whereas reducing conditions will show minimal protective oxide formation and accelerated surface compositional changes. In both cases, degradation (e.g., measured by loss of mechanical integrity and changes in microstructure near grain boundaries) will be more pronounced than in samples maintained in an inert baseline environment.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy state with an intact, homogeneous FCC matrix and minimal surface oxide prior to high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Effects are expected to be significant at temperatures around 900 °C and at gas compositions with high oxygen partial pressures versus environments with a strong reducing potential; deviations outside these conditions may show muted degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative rates of oxide scale formation, spallation, and subsequent microstructural degradation are not precisely known, and the interplay between the kinetics of grain boundary diffusion and thermal stress evolution introduces uncertainty in predicting exact time scales and degradation extents.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identically manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and expose them to high-temperature aging (e.g., 900 °C for up to 120 hours) under three atmospheres: a controlled oxidizing environment (e.g., 10 mbar O2), a reducing environment (e.g., H2-containing or low oxygen), and an inert environment (baseline). After exposure, use cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to evaluate the oxide scale morphology and composition across grain boundaries. Complement these observations with weight-gain measurements and mechanical testing (such as nanoindentation) to assess degradation.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of the oxide scale via TEM
Elemental mapping (especially of Cr, Al, and Ti) at grain boundary regions via EDS
Weight change (parabolic rate constant) during oxidation
Mechanical integrity tests (hardness, tensile strength) post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both oxidizing and reducing environments produce similar oxide scale characteristics (i.e., a uniform, stable oxide layer with no evidence of spallation or accelerated compositional degradation at grain boundaries) and similar mechanical performance compared to the inert baseline, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary-controlled, environment-dependent oxide scale instability governs degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of mixing equal or near equal amounts of elements to fabricate new alloys has sparked worldwide interest in alloy design. The approach is based on mixing multiple principal elements (MPE) in relatively high (often equiatomic) concentrations and stands in sharp contrast to the traditional practice of adding minor alloying elements. Though much emphasis is given to enhancing the mechanical properties while designing MPE alloys (MPEAs), understanding the corrosion and oxidation behavior of these alloys is an emerging research area. The MPEAs based on transition elements, such as CoCrFeNiMnAl (referred to as high entropy alloys or HEAs), have shown improved combinations of strength, ductility, and strain hardenability,. The structure and stability of HEAs surface oxides, however, are not well understood largely due to a wide variety of compositions and limited understanding of the underlying atomic-scale mechanisms of the oxidation process. Oxide formation tendencies in a liquid solution can thermodynamically be roughly deduced by Ellingham diagrams. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition.
